newsitem.title: THAILAND: Three monks said killed during Burma unrest.
newsitem.headline: Three monks said killed during Burma unrest.

text.p: Soldiers killed at least three Buddhist monks and arested 100 during recent religious unrest in Burma, a group of exiled monks said on Wednesday.

"At least three monks were shot dead by the SLORC (State Law and Order Restoration Council) security forces, and more than 100 monks were arrested, according to reliable sources," the All Burma Young Monk's Union (ABYMU) said in a statement obtained by Reuters in Bangkok.
The ABYMU is based on the Thai-Burma border and is loosely affiliated with other exiled Burmese groups.
The ABYMU, which accused the SLORC of stirring up religious unrest, did not say when the monks were killed.
Unrest between Buddhist monks and Moslems broke out in mid-March in Burma's second city Mandalay. Witnesses reported that several mosques were ransacked and the monks staged protests in the street.
The unrest, which spread to other cities including the capital Rangoon, led the SLORC to impose a curfew in Mandalay and heighten security across the country.

Witnesses in Rangoon said they saw at least 100 monks detained by authorities who brought them in trucks to an unused race course that in the past had served as a detention centre during periods of unrest.
The statement said the monks in Mandalay had originally planned to hold a demonstration on March 13 but were forced to postpone it when the SLORC learned of their plan.
It said after the unrest began around March 16, the monks in Mandalay held a meeting to discuss the deaths in prison of several monks who had been jailed.
Two SLORC officials arrived during the monks' meeting and stirred up religious conflict, the statement said.
The ABYMU said that despite the action by the Burmese troops the monks would continue their activities.

Buddhist monks played a key role in pro-democracy protests between 1988-1990. Thousands were detained after many monks refused to perform religious rights for soldiers or their families in 1990 following military crackdowns on the democracy movement.
SLORC officials have said no one was injured in the recent unrest and denied reports of the deaths of imprisoned monks.
